title: Attribute-Based and Resource-Based Authorization
learning_outcomes: Explain how attribute-based and resource-based authorization affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from ownership rules to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on attribute-based and resource-based authorization in authentication, authorization, and identity. You will connect ownership rules to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Attribute-Based and Resource-Based Authorization matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying ownership rules deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 121 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 121: Ownership rules → Tenant and organization boundaries → Attribute-based policies → Field-level permissions.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A credential may identify a caller; policy checks decide whether that caller can perform this operation on this resource. In this lesson, treat “Attribute-Based and Resource-Based Authorization” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Attribute-Based and Resource-Based Authorization
content_blocks.code:
GET /v1/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.test
Authorization: Bearer <short-lived-access-token>
Accept: application/json

# The server validates token signature/issuer/audience/expiry,
# then checks the caller's permission for this specific resource.
content_blocks.expected_output: A valid token authenticates a caller but does not automatically authorize every action or resource.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Ownership rules”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Tenant and organization boundaries” and “Field-level permissions”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Authentication establishes identity; authorization must still check the requested action and resource. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating attribute-based and resource-based authorization. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Ownership rules” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Attribute-Based and Resource-Based Authorization with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating attribute-based and resource-based authorization as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: A credential may identify a caller; policy checks decide whether that caller can perform this operation on this resource. In this lesson, treat “Attribute-Based and Resource-Based Authorization” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
